title: I’m an Australian-Palestinian doctor who was turned away at the West Bank border. The stigma of being born in Gaza stands in the way of peace
html:
This month I set out to return to Palestine, where I was born and studied, as part of a health diplomacy delegation to the occupied Palestinian territories and Israel. After two attempts at two separate border crossings, I was denied entry, despite an approved visa and an official invitation from the charity on whose board I sit, Rozana. The alleged reason is that I hold a Gaza ID, even though I haven’t lived there for 28 years.

Rozana trains Palestinian doctors and nurses in Israeli hospitals and transports patients from the West Bank and Gaza to critical care. My mission as a board director of Rozana Australia is to advocate for dialogue through healthcare collaboration. I have seen the power of this work up close, and I believe it can pave the way for Palestinians and Israelis to recognise their shared need for peace and security.

Nevertheless, I was turned away at the border. Multiple border agents failed to see the importance of the work I was travelling for. All they chose to see was my place of birth. The stigma of being born in Gaza stands in the way of peace and dignity, and at its core is the dehumanisation of Palestinians, judged by where we were born and nothing else. My experience was a reminder that the search for coexistence begins with equal rights and respect for our shared humanity.

I had also been invited to speak at Bethlehem University, my alma mater. It would have been my first visit since I graduated in 1996. If we fail to ground ourselves in our shared humanity, we surrender to the status quo of hate, fear and indefinite dispossession of the Palestinian people. So when the Israeli authorities told me to return home to Australia, I refused. Reality is too often imposed on Palestinians in the occupied territories, who have no control over their freedom of movement.

Instead, I travelled to Malta, a childhood dream, then sailed to Sicily and on to Venice, the resting place of my friend Faraj Wadi from Bethlehem University. Faraj died in 2003, and left behind an Italian wife and two Palestinian-Italian sons whom he had named Ishmael and Isaac.

He chose those names, the biblical forebears of the Jewish and Muslim peoples, because he so wanted Palestinians to be treated as equals of their Israeli cousins. Faraj never saw that dream realised in Gaza but he achieved it in his new home of Venice. Those of Faraj’s family who survived the past three years in Gaza would have dreamed of visiting the resting place of their son, to see that he had at least found equality and freedom there. In Gaza, too many to count are still to be recovered and buried after three years of mass destruction.

Standing there, at the final resting place of my friend from our home in Gaza, I was struck by the irony that neither of us had been permitted to return home, to the land of our birth. Neither of us was allowed the very freedom and equality that we fought for all people. Touring Malta and Italy was a moment of peace and recollection after a traumatic three years.

I return to this work today in Australia, committed to Rozana and to a path forward that builds equality, freedom and peace for all Palestinians and all Israelis. That will not be possible until we are able to find the common humanity in one another, or without ending the dehumanisation of people just like me, which sadly persists to this day at checkpoints and borders.

The path forward is simple. We must work together to achieve equality for both Palestinians and Israelis, and to end the segregation that persists in Israel and in Palestine. This can be done if we persist. If Ishmael and Isaac, the Italian-born sons of a Palestinian from Gaza, can meet their father’s friend, a Palestinian Australian, then surely it can be done for Israelis and Palestinians, who are separated by no more than a matter of kilometres.

Australia has a stake in this. The federal government has funded programs that bring senior Palestinian and Israeli health leaders together, and next month the royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion will report. Both depend on people being free to move and to be heard. Governments that fund this work should insist that the people doing it can cross the lines it is meant to bridge.

The world’s emerging leaders need to come together and help Palestinians and Israelis find a lasting peace in which our younger generations can coexist rather than carry on the burden of their parents. Such a future is currently being taken hostage by extremists from both sides, while ordinary Palestinian and Israeli mums and dads are silenced.

This piece is dedicated to Faraj’s memory. In Arabic, his name means awaiting relief after hardship.

  • Dr Munther Emad is a Palestinian Australian born in Gaza and a director of Rozana Australia. He writes in a personal capacity
